title: Periodic Variations in Element Properties
lead: The size of an atom, the energy needed to remove an electron from it and the energy change when it gains one all vary periodically with its electronic structure. Covalent and ionic radii, first and successive ionization energies, and electron affinities are followed across periods and down groups, with the effective nuclear charge as the guide.
objectives: Describe and explain the observed trends in atomic size, ionization energy, and electron affinity of the elements
summary_html: Electron configurations allow us to understand many periodic trends. Covalent radius increases as we move down a group because the n level (orbital size) increases. Covalent radius mostly decreases as we move left to right across a period because the effective nuclear charge experienced by the electrons increases, and the electrons are pulled in tighter to the nucleus. Anionic radii are larger than the parent atom, while cationic radii are smaller, because the number of valence electrons has changed while the nuclear charge has remained constant. Ionization energy (the energy associated with forming a cation) decreases down a group and mostly increases across a period because it is easier to remove an electron from a larger, higher energy orbital. Electron affinity (the energy associated with forming an anion) is more favorable (exothermic) when electrons are placed into lower energy orbitals, closer to the nucleus. Therefore, electron affinity becomes increasingly negative as we move left to right across the periodic table and decreases as we move down a group. For both IE and electron affinity data, there are exceptions to the trends when dealing with completely filled or half-filled subshells.

exercises.prompt: Give an example of an atom whose size is smaller than fluorine.
Which has the lowest value for IE<sub>1</sub>: O, Po, Pb, or Ba?
Based on their positions in the periodic table, predict which has the smallest atomic radius: Mg, Sr, Si, Cl, I.
Based on their positions in the periodic table, predict which has the largest atomic radius: Li, Rb, N, F, I.

answer.solution: Rb has the largest atomic radius. Radius increases down a group, because each step adds a shell with a larger principal quantum number, and it decreases from left to right across a period, because Zeff increases and draws the valence electrons closer to the nucleus. Li, N and F lie in period 2, while Rb and I lie in period 5, so Rb and I have an extra three shells and are larger than the other three. Rb is in group 1 and I in group 17 of the same period, so Rb, with the smaller effective nuclear charge, is the larger of the two. The covalent radii in Figure 6.30 agree: Rb 265 pm, Li 167 pm, I 133 pm, N 71 pm and F 64 pm.

exercises.prompt: Based on their positions in the periodic table, predict which has the largest first ionization energy: Mg, Ba, B, O, Te.
Based on their positions in the periodic table, predict which has the smallest first ionization energy: Li, Cs, N, F, I.

answer.solution: Cs has the smallest first ionization energy. $\kIE_{1}$ decreases down a group, because the outermost electron lies in a shell farther from the nucleus and is held less strongly, and it increases across a period as Zeff increases. Cs lies in group 1 like Li, but five periods lower, in period 6, so its 6s electron is the farthest from the nucleus of the five and feels the weakest pull. N and F are in period 2 to the right of Li, and I is in group 17, so all three hold their electrons more tightly. Figure 6.34 gives $\kIE_{1}$ = 380 kJ/mol for Cs, against 520 kJ/mol for Li, 1010 kJ/mol for I, 1400 kJ/mol for N and 1680 kJ/mol for F.

exercises.prompt: Based on their positions in the periodic table, rank the following atoms in order of increasing first ionization energy: F, Li, N, Rb
Based on their positions in the periodic table, rank the following atoms in order of increasing first ionization energy: Mg, O, S, Si

answer.solution: The order of increasing first ionization energy is Mg < Si < S < O. Mg, Si and S lie in period 3, in groups 2, 14 and 16, and $\kIE_{1}$ generally increases from left to right across a period because Zeff increases and the valence electrons are held more tightly, so Mg < Si < S. Oxygen lies directly above sulfur in group 16; its valence electrons are in the n = 2 shell, closer to the nucleus than the n = 3 electrons of sulfur, so O has the larger $\kIE_{1}$ and comes last. Figure 6.34 confirms the order: Mg 730 kJ/mol, Si 780 kJ/mol, S 1000 kJ/mol and O 1310 kJ/mol.

exercises.prompt: Based on their positions in the periodic table, list the following atoms in order of increasing radius: Mg, Ca, Rb, Cs.
Based on their positions in the periodic table, list the following atoms in order of increasing radius: Sr, Ca, Si, Cl.

answer.solution: The order of increasing radius is Cl < Si < Ca < Sr. Si and Cl lie in period 3, and radius decreases across a period as Zeff increases, so Cl, in group 17, is smaller than Si, in group 14. Ca and Sr lie in group 2, and radius increases down a group as the principal quantum number of the valence shell increases, so Sr, in period 5, is larger than Ca, in period 4. Ca has its valence electrons in the n = 4 shell, one shell beyond those of Si and Cl, and it is also far to the left of them, so it is larger than both. The covalent radii in Figure 6.30 agree: Cl 99 pm, Si 111 pm, Ca 176 pm and Sr 195 pm.

exercises.prompt: Based on their positions in the periodic table, list the following ions in order of increasing radius: K<sup>+</sup>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Al<sup>3+</sup>, Si<sup>4+</sup>.
List the following ions in order of increasing radius: Li<sup>+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup>, Br<sup>–</sup>, Te<sup>2–</sup>.

answer.solution: The order of increasing radius is Li+ < Mg2+ < Br– < Te2–. The electron configurations show the outermost shell of each ion: Li+ is 1s2, with n = 1; Mg2+ is 1s22s22p6, with n = 2; Br– is [Ar]3d104s24p6, with n = 4; and Te2– is [Kr]4d105s25p6, with n = 5. Each increase in the principal quantum number of the outermost electrons places them farther from the nucleus, so the size follows n. The two cations have lost their valence electrons and are smaller than their parent atoms, while the two anions have gained electrons, which increases the repulsion among them and lowers Zeff per electron, so they are larger than their parent atoms.

exercises.prompt: Which atom and/or ion is (are) isoelectronic with Br<sup>+</sup>: Se<sup>2+</sup>, Se, As<sup>–</sup>, Kr, Ga<sup>3+</sup>, Cl<sup>–</sup>?
Which of the following atoms and ions is (are) isoelectronic with S<sup>2+</sup>: Si<sup>4+</sup>, Cl<sup>3+</sup>, Ar, As<sup>3+</sup>, Si, Al<sup>3+</sup>?

answer.solution: Cl3+ and Si are isoelectronic with S2+. Sulfur has 16 electrons, so S2+ has 14, with the configuration [Ne]3s23p2. Counting the electrons of each species as its atomic number minus its charge gives Si4+, 14 − 4 = 10; Cl3+, 17 − 3 = 14; Ar, 18; As3+, 33 − 3 = 30; Si, 14; and Al3+, 13 − 3 = 10. Only Cl3+ and Si have 14 electrons, and both have the same configuration as S2+: a silicon atom is [Ne]3s23p2, and removing three 3p electrons from chlorine, [Ne]3s23p5, also leaves [Ne]3s23p2. Si4+ and Al3+ are isoelectronic with Ne instead.

exercises.prompt: Compare both the numbers of protons and electrons present in each to rank the following ions in order of increasing radius: As<sup>3–</sup>, Br<sup>–</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup>.

Of the five elements Al, Cl, I, Na, Rb, which has the most exothermic reaction? (E represents an atom.) What name is given to the energy for the reaction? (Hint: Note the process depicted does not correspond to electron affinity.) $\text{E}^{+}(g)+\text{e}^{-}\longrightarrow\text{E}(g)$

answer.solution: Cl has the most exothermic reaction, releasing 1250 kJ/mol, and the energy of the reaction is the negative of the first ionization energy, −$\kIE_{1}$. The process $\text{E}^{+}(g)+\text{e}^{-}\longrightarrow\text{E}(g)$ is the reverse of first ionization, $\text{E}(g)\longrightarrow\text{E}^{+}(g)+\text{e}^{-}$, so it releases the same energy that ionization absorbs. The element with the largest $\kIE_{1}$ therefore releases the most energy when its cation captures an electron. Of the five, Na and Rb are in group 1 and Al in group 13, all with low ionization energies, while Cl and I are in group 17; Cl lies above I, with its valence electrons in the smaller n = 3 shell, so it holds them most tightly. Figure 6.34 gives $\kIE_{1}$ = 1250 kJ/mol for Cl, 1010 kJ/mol for I, 580 kJ/mol for Al, 490 kJ/mol for Na and 400 kJ/mol for Rb.

exercises.prompt: Of the five elements Sn, Si, Sb, O, Te, which has the most endothermic reaction? (E represents an atom.) What name is given to the energy for the reaction? $\text{E}(g)\longrightarrow\text{E}^{+}(g)+\text{e}^{-}$

The ionic radii of the ions S<sup>2–</sup>, Cl<sup>–</sup>, and K<sup>+</sup> are 184, 181, 138 pm respectively. Explain why these ions have different sizes even though they contain the same number of electrons.

answer.solution: The three ions differ in size because their nuclei carry different charges. Each has 18 electrons in the configuration [Ne]3s23p6, so they are isoelectronic, and for isoelectronic species the number of protons determines the size. S2– has 16 protons, Cl– has 17 and K+ has 19. The same set of electrons, with the same shielding, therefore feels a larger Zeff from the potassium nucleus than from the chlorine nucleus, and the smallest from the sulfur nucleus. The stronger pull draws the electrons closer, so the radius falls as the nuclear charge rises: S2– is the largest at 184 pm, Cl– is 181 pm, and K+, with two more protons than chlorine, is the smallest at 138 pm.
